title: The First Civilisations · Episode 2
chapters: Tutankhamun: the tomb that time forgot
The Rosetta Stone: cracking the code of the pharaohs

units.t: The First Civilisations. Episode two.
In this episode: Tutankhamun: the tomb that time forgot, The Rosetta Stone: cracking the code of the pharaohs and The Indus Valley civilisation.
Part one. Tutankhamun: the tomb that time forgot.
He was a minor king who died as a teenager.
That is exactly why his tomb survived, and why its discovery in 1922 stunned the world.
The boy king.
Tutankhamun ruled Egypt for only about nine or ten years in the fourteenth century BC, coming to the throne at around eight or nine.
His father was very probably Akhenaten, the pharaoh who abandoned Egypt’s traditional gods to worship a single sun disc, the Aten.
The boy was originally named Tutankhaten, meaning living image of the Aten.
Early in his reign, guided by powerful advisers, the court restored the old gods, and his name was changed to Tutankhamun, honouring the god Amun.
He died at around eighteen or nineteen.
To later Egyptians, he was a footnote, and later kings even left his name off official lists.
Carter’s last season.
By the early twentieth century, most archaeologists believed the Valley of the Kings had given up all its secrets.
Howard Carter, an English archaeologist, disagreed.
Small finds bearing Tutankhamun’s name convinced him that the king’s tomb was still out there.
His sponsor, the fifth Earl of Carnarvon, was ready to stop paying by 1922, but Carter persuaded him to fund one final season.
On 4 November 1922, workers uncovered a stone step cut into the bedrock, leading to a sealed doorway.
On 26 November, Carter made a small hole and held up a candle.

Asked whether he could see anything, he later recalled replying that he could see wonderful things: gilded couches, statues, chests and chariots, in a room no one had entered for over three thousand years.
Robbed, but not emptied.
Tutankhamun’s tomb was not untouched.
Evidence showed that robbers broke in at least once, and probably twice, soon after the burial.
They took small, easily carried valuables such as oils and metal objects before officials found the break-in, tidied up and resealed it.
Then luck intervened.
Flood debris and the rubble and huts of workers digging later tombs, including that of Ramesses VI, buried the entrance, and it was forgotten.
The tomb itself was small, possibly a private tomb adapted in a hurry after his unexpected death.
Yet it held over five thousand objects, and recording, conserving and removing them took Carter and his team about a decade.
Gold, and much more.
The best known treasure is the funerary mask, made of gold inlaid with glass and semi-precious stones and weighing about ten kilograms.
The king’s body lay inside three nested coffins, the innermost of solid gold and weighing over a hundred kilograms, enclosed within a stone sarcophagus and four gilded wooden shrines.

But many of the most revealing objects were ordinary: chariots, bows, walking sticks, board games, linen underwear, sandals, jars of food and wine, and a lock of hair that belonged to his grandmother, Queen Tiye.
There were even two tiny mummified daughters, stillborn babies buried with their father.
Together these objects let historians see an Egyptian royal life in unusual detail.
The curse that wasn’t.
In April 1923, just months after the opening, Lord Carnarvon died in Cairo.
A mosquito bite, which he had accidentally nicked while shaving, became infected.
Newspapers competing for stories spread the idea of a pharaoh’s curse, and novelists such as Arthur Conan Doyle encouraged it.
No curse inscription was found in the tomb.
Howard Carter, who spent the most time inside, lived until 1939.
Later studies comparing people present at the opening with others found no sign that they died earlier.
How Tutankhamun himself died is still debated.
Scans and DNA studies have pointed to a broken leg, a foot deformity and evidence of malaria, but no single cause is agreed.
The key idea: Tutankhamun was a minor king who restored Egypt’s old gods and died at about eighteen or nineteen.
Part two. The Rosetta Stone: cracking the code of the pharaohs.
For fourteen centuries nobody on Earth could read an Egyptian hieroglyph.
Then a broken slab of stone and a stubborn young Frenchman changed everything.
A slab in a wall.
In July 1799, during Napoleon’s invasion of Egypt, French soldiers rebuilding a fort near Rashid, Rosetta, in the Nile Delta noticed a dark block covered in writing.
It was a broken slab of granodiorite, a little over a metre tall, with three bands of text.

The text was an ordinary decree from priests at Memphis in 196 BC, praising the young king Ptolemy V. What mattered was the format: hieroglyphs, Demotic, the everyday cursive script, and ancient Greek.
Scholars could read Greek, so it could act as a crib for the other two.
The British took the stone in 1801 under the terms of surrender, and it has been in the British Museum since 1802.
Why nobody could read it.
Hieroglyphs were used for over three thousand years, but as Egypt became part of the Greek, Roman and Christian world, fewer people learnt them.
The last known inscription was carved at the temple of Philae in AD 394, and the knowledge vanished.
For centuries, European scholars believed each picture stood for a deep idea.
In the seventeenth century, Athanasius Kircher published elaborate translations that were pure invention.
That assumption was the real barrier.
While people looked for hidden philosophy in every owl and reed, they could not see that many signs simply spelt out sounds, like letters.
Even with the Greek crib, cracking the code took more than twenty years.
Names in ovals.
Some hieroglyphs were enclosed in an oval ring, now called a cartouche.
Scholars suspected these held royal names.
In the 1810s, the English polymath Thomas Young, a physicist and doctor, showed that one cartouche matched the name Ptolemy in the Greek text, and he identified several sounds correctly.
But he believed sound signs were used mainly for foreign names.
Then a second inscription helped.
An obelisk from Philae carried the names Ptolemy and Cleopatra, which share the letters p, t, o and l.
Where the same signs spelt the shared sounds in both cartouches, even in different positions, that was strong evidence of an alphabet-like system.
Champollion’s leap.
Jean-François Champollion, a French linguist, had studied languages obsessively since boyhood, including Coptic, the late form of Egyptian still used in Christian church services.
In 1822, he studied cartouches copied from temples such as Abu Simbel.
One began with a sun disc.
In Coptic, the word for sun was ‘re’.
It ended with signs he already read as ‘s’, and between them was a sign he linked to the Coptic word for birth, ‘mise’.
Together they spelt Ramesses, a truly Egyptian pharaoh, not a Greek one.
Sound signs were used throughout the script.
A family story says he rushed to his brother’s office, cried that he had done it, and collapsed.
How the script works.
Champollion announced his results in a famous letter in September 1822, and the decades that followed confirmed and refined them.
Hieroglyphic writing proved to be a clever mixture.
Some signs stand for a single consonant, some for two or three consonants together, and some for a whole word.
Many words end with a silent sign called a determinative, which tells the reader what kind of thing is meant.
A pair of walking legs might mark a verb of movement, while a seated man marks a person.
Vowels were usually not written, which is why scholars still argue over how names were pronounced.
Once the system was understood, temple walls, tomb paintings and papyri could finally speak again.
The key idea: The Rosetta Stone carried one decree in three scripts, so readable Greek could unlock the unreadable Egyptian.
Part three. The Indus Valley civilisation.
Five thousand years ago, cities in modern Pakistan and India had grid streets and covered drains.
We still can't read their writing.
A forgotten civilisation.
Along the Indus River and its neighbours, in today's Pakistan and north-west India, a major civilisation arose around the same time as Egypt's pyramids.
It is also called the Harappan civilisation, after Harappa, the first site excavated.
It was forgotten for thousands of years until archaeologists recognised it in the 1920s, at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro.
At its height it covered a larger area than Egypt or Mesopotamia, with more than a thousand known settlements, from small villages to big cities such as Dholavira and Rakhigarhi.
Population estimates vary widely, but some scholars suggest several million people at its peak.
Planned cities, clean water.
Mohenjo-daro and Harappa had streets in a rough grid, with wide main roads and smaller lanes.
Bricks came in consistent proportions, roughly 1:2:4 for thickness, width and length, across hundreds of kilometres.
That suggests shared rules.
Many cities had a raised citadel with public buildings above a lower residential town.
Mohenjo-daro's Great Bath, about 12 metres long, was sealed with bitumen.
The water engineering was remarkable.
Mohenjo-daro may have had hundreds of brick-lined wells.
Many houses had bathing areas and toilets draining into covered brick sewers with inspection holes.
Dholavira, in a drier area, built large reservoirs for rainwater.
Few places had anything comparable for thousands of years.
Farmers, crafts and trade.
Most Indus people were farmers and herders, growing wheat, barley, peas and sesame.
They were among the earliest to grow cotton and weave it into cloth.
Craftspeople drilled long, polished carnelian beads, so prized that similar ones turn up in Mesopotamian royal tombs.
They also made painted pottery, copper and bronze tools, and clay toys.
Merchants traded cotton, beads, gems and timber by land and along the Arabian coast.
Mesopotamian texts mention a land called Meluhha, probably the Indus region.
Standardised cube-shaped stone weights, following a consistent system, suggest organised trade.
The port of Lothal had a large brick basin that many think was a dockyard.
Seals and a silent script.
Thousands of small square seals, often showing bulls, elephants or a one-horned beast, were probably pressed into clay to mark goods and their owners.
The one-horned animal, sometimes called a unicorn, is the most common image, and its meaning is unknown.
The seals carry short inscriptions.
Several thousand inscribed objects survive, using around 400 different signs, but most inscriptions are only about five signs long.
There is no long text and no bilingual inscription to act as a key, as the Rosetta Stone did for Egyptian.
Many decipherments have been proposed, but scholars accept none.
Most agree it was usually written right to left.
Until it is read, we don't know their language or any names.
Rulers and decline.
Unlike Egypt and Mesopotamia, Indus sites show no obvious palaces, grand royal tombs or monuments glorifying rulers.
A small stone bust nicknamed the 'Priest-King' may not show a king at all.
The gap between rich and poor seems smaller than elsewhere, and there are few signs of large-scale warfare.
Some scholars suggest power was shared, though absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence.
Over a few centuries, the big cities were gradually abandoned as people moved to smaller villages, especially eastward.
Leading explanations include a weakening monsoon, shifting rivers and less trade with Mesopotamia.
The old idea of a sudden invasion is no longer widely accepted.
Mohenjo-daro is now a UNESCO World Heritage site, threatened by salt and erosion.
The key idea: The Indus civilisation was as old as Egypt's pyramids and larger in area, yet it was forgotten until the 1920s.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What changed in Egyptian religion early in Tutankhamun’s reign?
Answer. The old gods were restored after Akhenaten.
Question two. Why was the Rosetta Stone so valuable to scholars?
Answer. One decree appeared in Greek, which they could read.
Question three. What was remarkable about the Indus civilisation's place in history?
Answer. As old as Egypt's pyramids but forgotten until the 1920s.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
